Evil Dead Burn Review — This One Hits Different (And Not How You Think)

short // Jul 12, 2026

Watch on YouTube

Evil Dead Burn is out, we caught it, and the short version is: it rips. Blood everywhere, Deadites in rare form, a theater full of people making noises they'd be embarrassed about in daylight. Good night out.

But somewhere in the third act it hit us — six movies deep, this franchise doesn't have a hero anymore. It has survivors. And that's a completely different thing.

What the New Era Absolutely Nails

Let's hand Burn its flowers first, because it earns them.

  • The action never lets up. It's chaotic, it's mean, and it moves.
  • The practical gore still lands like a truck. There's noticeably more CGI here than in previous entries and you will clock it — but when the real stuff shows up, it's top-tier.
  • The Deadites are perfect. Again.

That last one is the big one. Whatever else you want to argue about the modern era, it understands Deadites better than almost anything else in horror right now. The 2013 reboot got it. Evil Dead Rise got it. Burn gets it. That specific flavor of wrong — something wearing a person you love and clearly enjoying it — is fully intact.

If you came for a nasty time, you are getting a nasty time. No notes.

The Chosen One Problem

Here's what we couldn't shake.

The original run had Ash Williams, and Ash was the whole engine. Bruce Campbell built a character who could get his own hand possessed, lose an argument with his reflection, get bullied by tiny versions of himself, and then say something spectacularly stupid before cutting a Deadite in half with a boomstick. High-concept horror and slapstick running at the same time, somehow both working.

That was the identity. Not just the gore — the swagger.

The new era traded all of it for bleak family trauma. Which is effective, fine. But it means every entry now runs the same shape: ordinary people, terrible night, wolves in familiar clothing, try to make it to sunrise. Nobody's chosen. Nobody's got a destiny. There's no character carrying you from one film into the next.

Six entries in, that absence is starting to echo.

About That Bruce Campbell Cameo

Yes, he's in it. No, not the way you want.

Instead of putting Ash back on screen, Burn puts Bruce's photo on a wall, quietly watching over the characters. It's a cute easter egg and the crowd we saw it with popped for it.

It also stung. Because the second you put him on that wall, you're reminding everybody exactly what these films don't have anymore — and then walking straight past it. If you're going to gesture at the king, gesture harder.

That was the return we were most curious about, and it's the one that let us down.

How the Leaks Held Up

Before release we went through every alleged leak from those L.A. test screenings and sorted the real intel from the fan fiction wearing a trench coat. Now that the movie's actually out, that scorecard reads pretty well — the stuff we marked confirmed landed just about exactly as described.

The XFD Bottom Line

Evil Dead Burn is a genuinely good, genuinely brutal horror movie, and if the modern era is what you signed up for, this is one of its better nights out.

But it leaves the franchise standing at a crossroads it keeps refusing to pick a side of: full survival dread, or the horror-comedy swagger that made this name legendary in the first place. Right now it's doing one of those extremely well and the other not at all.

So tell us straight — do you miss the Ash era, or is the Deadite-first modern run exactly what you want out of Evil Dead? We're settling this in the comments.

Stay nasty.
